title: Ridgeline plots: compare distributions without hiding their size
summary: Use shared units and smoothing, disclose whether each ridge has unit area, and make overlaps readable.
body:
Use shared units and smoothing, disclose whether each ridge has unit area, and make overlaps readable.

First decide what height means

A ridgeline plot stacks several distribution curves along one shared horizontal measure. Each ridge can be a normalized density or a count-scaled curve. Those choices answer different questions. Unit-area curves compare shape but erase group size; count-scaled curves retain volume but can bury small groups. Put the choice beside the chart and list group counts. A ridge with 47 observations should not appear as equally well supported as one with 4,700 just because both curves reach the same height. Box and violin displays offer a less overlapping alternative when the group count grows.

One bandwidth across comparable groups

A density ridge depends on the smoothing bandwidth. A narrow bandwidth can turn individual observations into false-looking peaks; a wide one can erase real mixtures. If the goal is comparison, use one documented bandwidth in the same units for every group, then inspect the underlying counts and a histogram or ECDF. Near a hard lower bound such as zero minutes, a symmetric kernel can place visual density below zero. Clip display only with an explicit boundary rule, or use a boundary-aware estimator. ECDFs avoid bandwidth choice entirely and are useful for checking tail claims.

Overlap is a design parameter

The vertical offset between ridges changes what is concealed. With heavy overlap, the front ridge can cover a smaller peak in the ridge behind it. Keep a thin outline, enough transparency and a stable layer order. Do not use color alone for identity; label each ridge on its own baseline. For a screen reader or a small phone, publish a companion table of group size, median and selected percentiles. Accessible chart alternatives help preserve the comparison when curves cannot be seen or hovered.

Keep populations and windows aligned

A weekly ridge may show an apparent shift because the eligible population changed, not because individual values moved. Define the event, unit, missing-value rule and period before comparing curves. If a week has too few valid observations, mark it as insufficient rather than creating a smooth curve from a handful of points. Keep the horizontal domain fixed across a report; otherwise a later ridge can look compressed only because its axis changed. Aggregation grain and period completeness should accompany the exported chart data.

Worked contract

from math import exp, isfinite, pi, sqrt

def gaussian_ridge(samples: list[float], grid: list[float],
                   bandwidth: float) -> list[float]:
    if not samples or not grid or not isfinite(bandwidth) or bandwidth <= 0:
        raise ValueError("samples, grid and positive bandwidth required")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in samples + grid):
        raise ValueError("values must be finite")
    scale = len(samples) * bandwidth * sqrt(2 * pi)
    return [sum(exp(-0.5 * ((position - value) / bandwidth) ** 2)
                for value in samples) / scale for position in grid]

weekly_minutes = {"week 47": [27, 31, 35, 41],
                  "week 48": [31, 37, 43, 49]}
grid_minutes = [30, 40, 50]
ridge_rows = {week: gaussian_ridge(values, grid_minutes, 8)
              for week, values in weekly_minutes.items()}
assert len(ridge_rows["week 47"]) == 3
assert all(height > 0 for heights in ridge_rows.values() for height in heights)
assert ridge_rows["week 47"][0] > ridge_rows["week 48"][0]

Performance and operating cost

For G groups, M grid positions and N total observations, direct Gaussian evaluation takes O(MN) time and O(GM) output space. The sample lists also occupy O(N) memory. A histogram convolution or a vetted density library is preferable for a very large grid. The code estimates unbounded Gaussian densities; it does not correct a physical zero boundary or choose a statistically justified bandwidth. Save the bandwidth, group counts, grid and raw eligibility rule with every export.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading equal-height, unit-area ridges as equal numbers of events.
  • Using a different automatic bandwidth for each group while comparing peaks.
  • Allowing overlap to hide a smaller group without outlines or a table.
  • Treating a four-record smooth curve as stable evidence of several modes.

Validation drill

Compare 59 weekly response-time groups. Mark weeks with fewer than 47 valid records, hold the unit and horizontal range fixed, and verify one apparent tail shift with an ECDF.

title: Regression overlays: separate fitted trend from individual spread
summary: Fit on a declared population, show the data behind the line, and keep confidence and prediction bands distinct.
body:
Fit on a declared population, show the data behind the line, and keep confidence and prediction bands distinct.

Define the fit population

A line on a scatterplot is a model output, not a property of the pixels. State which rows entered the fit, the x and y units, the time window and exclusions. If the visible chart filters to one region while the line is still fitted across all regions, label that difference or refit intentionally. A pooled line can hide opposing group trends. Plot groups separately before deciding whether a shared slope is defensible. Overplotting and sampling can make a line look better supported than the visible points imply.

Do not mix two kinds of band

A confidence band for the conditional mean describes uncertainty in the estimated average curve under the model. A prediction band for a new observation includes individual variation and is normally wider. Label the band type, level and fitting method; never call an arbitrary shaded region a confidence interval. Interval endpoints should be retained in the exported data. A narrow mean band does not promise that the next delivery will land near the line.

Check influential points and model shape

One distant x value may pull a straight line through a cloud that otherwise has little trend. Inspect residuals and report the fit's valid x range. If the relationship bends, a straight line can be a poor summary even when it is easy to draw. Do not extend the overlay far beyond observed x values unless extrapolation is the explicit task and its uncertainty is shown. Q–Q diagnostics can reveal distribution departures in residuals but do not repair confounding or nonlinearity.

Keep explanation separate from causation

A rising line means the plotted variables co-vary in the selected records. It does not establish that changing x will change y. Annotate outages, policy changes or cohorts where they matter, but do not turn temporal coincidence into a mechanism. Event annotations have the same limit. Publish the coefficients and row count alongside the plot, and offer a table of fitted values if the chart is interactive. A model revision should change its version in the export so the old and new lines can be reproduced.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def fit_straight_line(points: list[tuple[float, float]]) -> tuple[float, float]:
    if len(points) < 3 or any(not (isfinite(x) and isfinite(y))
                              for x, y in points):
        raise ValueError("at least three finite pairs required")
    mean_x = sum(x for x, _ in points) / len(points)
    mean_y = sum(y for _, y in points) / len(points)
    xx = sum((x - mean_x) ** 2 for x, _ in points)
    if xx == 0:
        raise ValueError("x values need variation")
    slope = sum((x - mean_x) * (y - mean_y) for x, y in points) / xx
    return mean_y - slope * mean_x, slope

dispatch_records = [(2, 47), (3, 59), (4, 71), (5, 83)]
intercept, slope = fit_straight_line(dispatch_records)
assert (intercept, slope) == (23.0, 12.0)
assert intercept + slope * 6 == 95.0

Performance and operating cost

Computing a simple least-squares line takes O(N) time and O(1) extra space for N pairs. The code deliberately does not calculate uncertainty bands: those require a named model, assumptions, residual variance and an interval method. It is only a descriptive fit; the four exact points are a code check, not evidence of predictive accuracy. Keep the raw rows or an auditable snapshot when shipping a chart with a fitted overlay.

Common Mistakes

  • Fitting on all rows while displaying only a filtered subset without saying so.
  • Calling a mean-confidence band a prediction interval for the next record.
  • Extrapolating a straight line beyond observed x values as though support were unchanged.
  • Interpreting an association line as proof of a causal effect.

Validation drill

Fit dispatch delay against queue depth for 188 records. Compare pooled and depot-specific slopes, identify the most influential record, and label any uncertainty band with its exact meaning.

title: Map boundaries: handle antimeridian crossings before drawing routes
summary: Normalize longitude, split crossings and treat projection distance as a display property.
body:
Normalize longitude, split crossings and treat projection distance as a display property.

Longitude has a seam

A route from 177 degrees east to 178 degrees west crosses a narrow part of the Pacific. A renderer that simply connects numeric longitudes may draw a line across nearly the entire map. Choose a longitude convention, validate it at ingestion, and split a crossing before sending geometry to the visual layer. Keep the original coordinates as well as display segments. Symbol maps also need a clear coordinate meaning; a route line needs the additional seam rule.

A bounding box can wrap

For an antimeridian-spanning area, a western longitude numerically greater than the eastern longitude can describe a small region. Do not automatically swap the two values or calculate width by direct subtraction. Compute wrapped angular span and tell a mapping library whether its viewport crosses the seam. A naive min-to-max bounding box may zoom to almost the whole world. Region boundaries need the same care when a polygon is split into multiple pieces for display.

Projection changes visual geometry

A flat map projects a curved surface. Pixel distance, area and direction can vary with projection and latitude. Use a projection appropriate to the question, and avoid estimating physical travel distance with screen coordinates. A straight segment drawn in longitude and latitude is not automatically the shortest path on Earth. When a route represents measured travel, retain the actual track; when it represents an abstract connection, label it as such. Scale integrity applies to maps as well as charts.

Preserve identity across pieces

After a crossing is cut into two display segments, both pieces must retain one route ID so a tooltip, filter and export refer to the same underlying trip. A segment count is not a trip count. Include source coordinate order, time zone for event timestamps, geometry version and wrapping method in the export. Test endpoints exactly at positive and negative 180 degrees. The export manifest should record enough to reproduce the same viewport and splitting rule after a map library upgrade.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def split_dateline_segment(west: tuple[float, float],
                           east: tuple[float, float]
                          ) -> list[list[tuple[float, float]]]:
    lon_a, lat_a = west
    lon_b, lat_b = east
    if not all(isfinite(value) for value in (*west, *east)):
        raise ValueError("coordinates must be finite")
    if not (-180 <= lon_a <= 180 and -180 <= lon_b <= 180
            and -90 <= lat_a <= 90 and -90 <= lat_b <= 90):
        raise ValueError("longitude or latitude outside range")
    difference = lon_b - lon_a
    if abs(difference) <= 180:
        return [[west, east]]
    adjusted_b = lon_b - 360 if difference > 180 else lon_b + 360
    seam = -180 if adjusted_b < lon_a else 180
    fraction = (seam - lon_a) / (adjusted_b - lon_a)
    seam_lat = lat_a + fraction * (lat_b - lat_a)
    opposite = 180 if seam == -180 else -180
    return [[west, (seam, seam_lat)], [(opposite, seam_lat), east]]

shipping_route = split_dateline_segment((177, -17), (-178, -18))
assert shipping_route == [
    [(177, -17), (180, -17.6)],
    [(-180, -17.6), (-178, -18)],
]

Performance and operating cost

Splitting one two-point segment is O(1) time and space; a route with N points needs O(N) processing and output. The interpolation is linear in longitude and latitude for display geometry, not a geodesic calculation. For long-distance navigation or polar tracks, densify with a suitable geographic method before projecting. A production pipeline must define how exact-seam endpoints, multi-segment tracks and duplicate 180-degree coordinates are serialized.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a nearly global line between two points that are close across the seam.
  • Swapping wrapped bounding-box longitudes and accidentally selecting most of the world.
  • Measuring real distance from flat-map pixels.
  • Counting two rendered pieces as two journeys.

Validation drill

Draw 47 shipping tracks with three seam crossings. Keep one ID per journey, verify wrapped viewport width, and compare the exported track length with the number of display segments.

title: Event-aligned charts: choose a baseline before comparing trajectories
summary: Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.
body:
Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.

Event time is not calendar time

An event-aligned chart puts each subject's event at relative time zero. This lets a reader compare trajectories before and after events that occurred on different calendar dates. Store the actual event timestamp as well as the relative offset; otherwise seasonality, outages and policy changes disappear. Specify whether an offset means elapsed hours, calendar days or complete reporting periods. Time-series period rules are essential when the event occurs late in a day or across a daylight-saving change.

Fix the baseline rule

A common display subtracts each subject's pre-event value or divides by it. These produce different shapes and units. Select the baseline window before inspecting outcomes, report how many valid observations contributed to it, and reject a percentage change when the baseline is zero. If one subject has only one pre-event measurement and another has 47, their aligned curves carry different reliability. Denominator and grain rules should stay visible with the chart. Plot absolute values alongside normalized values when the magnitude of the original series matters.

Missing is not flat

Do not fill missing pre-event days with the baseline or connect a line across an unobserved outage without a marker. A cohort average at relative day five may use fewer subjects than at day one because follow-up ends; show the contributing count by offset. Attrition can make a trend look like improvement. Small-sample uncertainty belongs near sparse tails, and forecast intervals must not be substituted for missing actual observations.

The line does not prove an effect

A change at time zero can reflect selection into the event, a concurrent intervention, regression to the mean or ordinary seasonality. An annotation identifies timing, not causality. Compare a relevant untreated group or a pre-specified benchmark if the decision requires an effect estimate, and state the assumptions of that comparison. Annotation and causal-claim boundaries apply here. Export subject ID, event date, relative offset, original value, baseline window, normalized value and eligibility state so every plotted line can be reconstructed.

Worked contract

from datetime import date
from math import isfinite

def event_aligned_change(event_day: date, observations: dict[date, float],
                         baseline_days: tuple[date, ...]
                        ) -> list[tuple[int, float, float]]:
    if not baseline_days or len(set(baseline_days)) != len(baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline days must be distinct")
    if any(day >= event_day or day not in observations for day in baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline must be observed before the event")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in observations.values()):
        raise ValueError("observations must be finite")
    baseline = sum(observations[day] for day in baseline_days) / len(baseline_days)
    return sorted(((day - event_day).days, value, value - baseline)
                  for day, value in observations.items())

incident_counts = {
    date(2026, 10, 5): 47, date(2026, 10, 6): 59,
    date(2026, 10, 8): 38, date(2026, 10, 9): 35,
}
aligned = event_aligned_change(
    date(2026, 10, 7), incident_counts,
    (date(2026, 10, 5), date(2026, 10, 6)),
)
assert aligned == [(-2, 47, -6), (-1, 59, 6), (1, 38, -15), (2, 35, -18)]
assert all(offset != 0 for offset, _, _ in aligned)

Performance and operating cost

For N observations and B baseline days, validation and averaging take O(N+B) time; sorting relative periods takes O(N log N) time and O(N) output space. The function leaves missing event day zero absent instead of inventing a value. Calendar dates are appropriate only when day-level reporting is the contract; intraday events need zoned timestamps and a declared binning method. Subtracting a baseline describes change, not a causal estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Discarding calendar dates after alignment and losing concurrent-event context.
  • Choosing a favorable baseline window after seeing the result.
  • Drawing a continuous line over days with no observations.
  • Calling a post-event change proof that the event caused it.

Validation drill

Align 81 facilities around a maintenance intervention. Show each facility's baseline window and post-event coverage, then recompute the cohort curve using only facilities observed through day 14.

title: Interactive charts: make selection work without a pointer
summary: Treat focus, selection and the data table as part of the chart's public interface.
body:
Treat focus, selection and the data table as part of the chart's public interface.

Hover is not access

A tooltip visible only on pointer hover excludes keyboard and many touch users. Give each interactive mark a reachable focus target, a meaningful accessible name and the same detail on focus as on hover. Arrow keys can move within a series, while Home and End can jump to its bounds; publish the key rules next to the chart. Keep a visible focus indicator. Color and text alternatives cover the static layer, but a chart with filters and selections also needs an interaction contract.

Separate focus from selection

Focus says where keyboard input will act. Selection says which records are included in the current analysis. Do not silently change the filter merely because focus moved to another point. If Enter selects a point, announce the new selection and update the related table or summary. A selected range should survive a resize and a redraw by stable record IDs rather than pixel coordinates. Linked filters and cohort state should make the selected population and denominator visible across all charts.

Avoid a thousand tab stops

Putting every mark in the page's normal Tab sequence can make a dense chart unusable. A single chart entry point followed by arrow-key movement may be better, provided the active point's name and value are exposed, the user can exit with Tab, and the navigation order is predictable. Do not trap focus inside the plot. For large series, offer direct search, a bounded table, or a downloadable data file so a user does not have to press an arrow 4,700 times. Large-series reduction must preserve access to underlying records when visual points are aggregated.

The table is a first-class view

An accessible data table should use the same filters, units, missing-value markers and ordering as the chart. If the chart displays a sampled or binned series, identify that fact and provide a route to full records when appropriate. Do not generate a table from SVG positions; derive both views from one data model. Export provenance should include the selection, filter and sort state so a shared screenshot and a CSV tell the same story. Test with only a keyboard, at narrow width, and with zoom before publication.

Worked contract

function nextChartPoint(currentIndex, pointCount, key) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(pointCount) || pointCount < 1 ||
      !Number.isInteger(currentIndex) || currentIndex < 0 ||
      currentIndex >= pointCount) {
    throw new RangeError("chart point state is invalid");
  }
  if (key === "ArrowRight" || key === "ArrowDown") {
    return Math.min(currentIndex + 1, pointCount - 1);
  }
  if (key === "ArrowLeft" || key === "ArrowUp") {
    return Math.max(currentIndex - 1, 0);
  }
  if (key === "Home") return 0;
  if (key === "End") return pointCount - 1;
  return currentIndex;
}

const visibleRecordIds = ["depot-47", "depot-59", "depot-83"];
let focusedIndex = 0;
focusedIndex = nextChartPoint(focusedIndex, visibleRecordIds.length, "End");
if (visibleRecordIds[focusedIndex] !== "depot-83") {
  throw new Error("keyboard focus must follow chart order");
}
if (nextChartPoint(focusedIndex, visibleRecordIds.length, "ArrowRight") !== 2) {
  throw new Error("focus must stop at the last record");
}

Performance and operating cost

A key transition takes O(1) time and space; the displayed order and accessible table require O(N) record storage for N visible points. The pure function handles movement only. The browser component must connect it to focus, accessible names, announcement text and selection state, and must retain Tab exit. If a virtualized chart reorders records, map stable IDs to the new order before restoring focus. Treat the table as the source-aligned view, not as a decorative duplicate.

Common Mistakes

  • Making hover-only tooltip content unavailable on focus and touch.
  • Changing the selected cohort whenever a user merely moves focus.
  • Adding every dense-series mark to the Tab order with no shortcut or data table.
  • Restoring focus by pixel position after filter changes instead of stable record identity.

Validation drill

Audit a 188-point chart using only keyboard navigation. Verify focus visibility, Enter selection, Tab exit, a synchronized table and stable record identity after a filter change.

title: Box and violin charts: compare groups without inventing density
summary: Keep sample size, quartiles and bandwidth visible when a smoothed shape represents observations.
body:
Keep sample size, quartiles and bandwidth visible when a smoothed shape represents observations.

Begin with observations

A box summarizes a group's quartiles and median; a violin adds an estimated density shape. Neither replaces the sample size. A smooth violin made from seven delivery times can look as confident as one made from seven thousand. Put each group's count beside its label and show individual points for small groups. Distribution and outlier displays explain what the summary hides. First check whether groups cover the same window, unit and eligibility rule. Otherwise the apparent difference may be a cohort change.

Declare the quartile rule

Software packages can interpolate quartiles differently, and whiskers may mean the extrema or a multiple of the interquartile range. State the rule in the chart caption or export record. A point beyond a whisker is not automatically bad data; it is flagged under that rule. If the decision needs the fraction exceeding a service threshold, calculate that fraction directly rather than asking a box to imply it. An empirical CDF answers threshold questions without a smoothing choice.

Treat bandwidth as a parameter

A violin's width depends on a density estimate and its bandwidth. A wide bandwidth can merge two real modes; a narrow one can turn routine noise into several peaks. Compare more than one defensible bandwidth, retain a rug or points, and do not imply that a thin tail continues beyond a physical limit. The mirrored shape is a drawing convention, not a second population. Normalize violin widths by count only if width should carry count. Otherwise make widths equal and show counts separately. Grain and denominator still matter.

Keep groups comparable

Use the same quantitative axis, bandwidth rule and density normalization across groups. Truncating each group to its own range can make spreads seem alike. For latency data, inspect zeros, censored values and caps before estimating density. If the data include repeated readings from the same device, an independent violin discards pairing. A paired view retains it. Supply a text table with each count, median, quartiles and threshold exceedance for readers who cannot use the shape.

Worked contract

def quartile_summary(readings: list[float]) -> dict[str, float | int]:
    from math import isfinite
    if not readings or any(not isfinite(value) for value in readings):
        raise ValueError("readings must be finite and nonempty")
    ordered = sorted(readings)
    def midpoint(values: list[float]) -> float:
        middle = len(values) // 2
        return (values[middle] if len(values) % 2 else
                (values[middle - 1] + values[middle]) / 2)
    middle = len(ordered) // 2
    lower = ordered[:middle]
    upper = ordered[middle + len(ordered) % 2:]
    return {"count": len(ordered), "median": midpoint(ordered),
            "q1": midpoint(lower) if lower else ordered[0],
            "q3": midpoint(upper) if upper else ordered[0]}

depot_latency = quartile_summary([47, 51, 59, 68, 81, 83, 96])
assert depot_latency == {"count": 7, "median": 68, "q1": 51, "q3": 83}

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N observations costs O(N log N) time and O(N) storage for the ordered copy. A chart with G groups repeats this per group; density estimation adds work set by the estimator and evaluation grid. The code declares a median-of-halves quartile convention and handles a one-item group. It does not draw a violin or claim that seven points support a smooth density. Store the exact convention with the exported summary.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a smooth violin for a tiny group without points.
  • Comparing boxes whose whiskers use different rules.
  • Treating a flagged point as an invalid measurement.
  • Changing density bandwidth between groups and reading widths as a real difference.

Validation drill

Compare response times for three depots with 7, 47 and 810 records. Print each count, median and quartile rule; draw points for the smallest group, then inspect whether two bandwidth choices alter the visual claim.

title: Empirical CDFs: read thresholds and tails without choosing bins
summary: Construct a cumulative distribution from observed values, preserving ties and sample size.
body:
Construct a cumulative distribution from observed values, preserving ties and sample size.

The step answers a threshold question

An empirical cumulative distribution function, or ECDF, gives the fraction of observed values less than or equal to each threshold. A point at 47 minutes and 0.8 means 80 percent of observations took at most 47 minutes. Unlike a histogram, it needs no bin width, so comparisons across groups are less sensitive to display choices. It still depends on the population, missing-value policy and observation window. Distribution plots should expose those rules before any percentile is interpreted.

Ties produce one jump

Repeated measurements at the same value create one larger step. If 31 of 81 jobs finish at exactly 12 minutes, the ECDF rises by 31/81 there; do not create a fake continuous slope between identical values. To compute a nearest-rank percentile, choose the first observed value whose cumulative share meets or exceeds the requested probability. Other quantile conventions interpolate and can return a number no job achieved. State the convention, especially for service targets. Sampling rules determine whether a percentile describes all jobs or a selected frame.

Keep the tail visible

Most observations can cluster near a short duration while a few long delays drive customer pain. An ECDF makes the proportion under a service threshold easy to read, but the far-right tail may still be squeezed by the axis. Add an inset, tail table or direct threshold counts when the rare cases matter. A survival-style complementary curve, one minus the ECDF, answers what fraction exceeds a threshold; be clear about strict versus inclusive inequalities at ties. Small samples need counts beside smooth-looking curves.

Compare only compatible cohorts

Two curves can differ because of case mix, eligibility, time window or measurement precision. Use consistent axis limits and units, label sample sizes, and show whether pending cases were excluded or censored. A naive ECDF of only completed jobs makes the slow unfinished work disappear. For a queue with unresolved jobs, use an analysis that handles censoring or restrict the claim to completed jobs. Observation status is part of the underlying data, not a cosmetic legend choice.

Worked contract

from math import ceil, isfinite

def completion_ecdf(minutes: list[float]) -> list[tuple[float, int, float]]:
    if not minutes or any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in minutes):
        raise ValueError("need finite nonnegative durations")
    ordered = sorted(minutes)
    steps = []
    for value in ordered:
        if steps and steps[-1][0] == value:
            steps[-1] = (value, steps[-1][1] + 1, 0.0)
        else:
            steps.append((value, 1, 0.0))
    cumulative = 0
    result = []
    for value, tied, _ in steps:
        cumulative += tied
        result.append((value, tied, cumulative / len(ordered)))
    return result

durations = [12, 12, 31, 47, 81]
curve = completion_ecdf(durations)
nearest_rank_80 = sorted(durations)[ceil(0.8 * len(durations)) - 1]
assert curve[0] == (12, 2, 0.4)
assert curve[-1][2] == 1.0 and nearest_rank_80 == 47

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N durations costs O(N log N) time and O(N) space for the ordered copy and output; scanning ties is O(N). Already-sorted warehouse output avoids the local sort. A chart with many distinct observations may still need visual reduction at screen resolution, but threshold queries should use the exact ordered values. The simple ECDF treats every supplied duration as complete and equally weighted; it is not a censored-data estimator.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading a completed-only ECDF as the distribution of all started jobs.
  • Treating a large jump at a tied value as a renderer defect.
  • Quoting a percentile without its sample size and quantile convention.
  • Moving axis bounds between cohorts and comparing apparent steepness.

Validation drill

Build curves for two depot cohorts of 47 and 81 completed cases. Include repeated durations and unresolved work, then report the fraction within 31 minutes and exactly which cases were excluded.

title: Dense scatterplots: reveal overlap without hiding rare observations
summary: Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.
body:
Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.

Overplotting changes what a point means

A scatterplot maps paired values to two position channels. When thousands of records land on the same pixels, the visible mark count no longer approximates the record count. Transparency can expose a dense center, but repeated strokes saturate and rare points can disappear beneath it. Before changing the mark style, count records per screen-space cell and inspect whether the question is about density, outliers, groups or exact cases. The chart question determines whether a point cloud is still the right view.

Bin at a declared resolution

A two-dimensional density grid counts observations inside fixed x and y intervals. It can show population structure without rendering every dot. The cells need axis units, bounds and bin width; changing cell size changes the picture. A cell count is not a probability unless divided by the declared population or area. Use the same grid for comparisons across cohorts, otherwise apparent hot spots may be a change in binning. Preserve a drill-down path to the original records where access rules permit it. A heatmap of density has the same color-domain obligations as any other heatmap.

Sampling is a data product

Uniform sampling can make a common cluster readable yet omit a rare but important failure mode. If the operational question concerns unusual refunds, retain those cases deliberately and label the sample design. A stratified sample can hold a fixed number from each category, but its plotted mix no longer reflects population proportions unless weights or counts are shown. Never present sampled points as the full dataset. Record the random seed, inclusion rule and population size. The sampling frame matters even when the result is only exploratory.

Separate trend from uncertainty

A diagonal cloud does not by itself establish a causal effect. Outliers, groups and repeated measures can alter the apparent slope. Show marginal distributions or group facets when one cluster masks another. If a fitted trend is added, distinguish raw marks from the fitted line and state whether the fit is weighted, filtered or calculated on the visible sample. Influence checks are needed before treating that line as a stable summary. A truncated axis can also make a weak relation seem strong.

Validate at the pixel budget

Test identical coordinates, boundary points, non-finite values and a small rare cohort. Count how many records end in each visible density cell, then reconcile the total with the filtered input. Hovering a cell should report its count and ranges, not invent a single representative record. At high density, compare a grid and a sampled-point layer side by side: the grid describes mass, while the points retain individual exceptions. On a small screen, favor one readable layer over simultaneous translucent layers that obscure both.

Worked contract

from math import floor, isfinite

def density_cells(points: list[tuple[float, float]],
                  x_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  y_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  columns: int, rows: int) -> dict[tuple[int, int], int]:
    x_low, x_high = x_bounds
    y_low, y_high = y_bounds
    if columns < 1 or rows < 1 or x_low >= x_high or y_low >= y_high:
        raise ValueError("invalid grid")
    counts: dict[tuple[int, int], int] = {}
    for amount, handling_minutes in points:
        if not all(map(isfinite, (amount, handling_minutes))):
            raise ValueError("non-finite observation")
        if not (x_low <= amount <= x_high and
                y_low <= handling_minutes <= y_high):
            raise ValueError("point outside declared domain")
        column = min(columns - 1, floor((amount - x_low) * columns / (x_high - x_low)))
        row = min(rows - 1, floor((handling_minutes - y_low) * rows / (y_high - y_low)))
        counts[(column, row)] = counts.get((column, row), 0) + 1
    return counts

cells = density_cells([(47, 18), (47, 18), (81, 39)],
                      (0, 100), (0, 50), 5, 5)
assert sum(cells.values()) == 3 and max(cells.values()) == 2

Performance and operating cost

For N points and C occupied cells, fixed-grid counting takes O(N) time and O(C) memory, with C no larger than the number of grid positions. Rendering one rectangle per occupied cell can be much cheaper than rendering N circles. The example rejects out-of-domain points; a production view may instead maintain an explicit overflow bucket, but it must label that choice. Recompute bins when the axis domain or pixel resolution changes, and do not confuse screen-density counts with a probability density estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Lowering opacity and assuming the visible marks still represent all records.
  • Sampling rare cases away while evaluating an exception-handling workflow.
  • Comparing density grids built with different bounds or cell widths.
  • Calling a fitted slope causal based on a crowded scatterplot.

Validation drill

Generate 4,700 routine handling cases plus 31 rare high-delay cases. Compare raw points, a fixed grid and a seeded stratified sample; report whether each view keeps the rare cluster visible and whether displayed counts reconcile.

title: Asymmetric error bars: tell readers what each endpoint means
summary: Carry lower and upper endpoints with every estimate, and never relabel arbitrary spread as uncertainty.
body:
Carry lower and upper endpoints with every estimate, and never relabel arbitrary spread as uncertainty.

The interval needs a type

An error bar may encode a standard deviation, a confidence interval, a prediction interval, an instrument tolerance or a minimum-to-maximum range. These answer different questions. Put the interval type, level where applicable, method and sample size in the chart caption. Uncertainty displays explain why a narrow-looking interval does not automatically mean a precise individual prediction. A bar without that contract invites the reader to supply the wrong interpretation. If the calculation is model-based, identify the population and conditions under which it applies.

Keep the endpoints, not just a radius

Some intervals are asymmetric around the estimate, especially near natural boundaries or after a nonlinear transform. Export estimate, lower and upper as three separate numbers. A renderer may ask for downward and upward distances, which can be derived from those endpoints without losing meaning. An estimate outside its own stated interval is a data error for many common interval definitions and should be stopped or explained. Forecast fan charts make this distinction even more important because uncertainty often widens with horizon.

Draw limits honestly

If an endpoint falls beyond the plotted axis, do not clip it silently. Extend the axis, use a visible arrow with the endpoint value, or choose another layout. A log axis cannot display zero or negative endpoints; transforming the point and interval requires the same transformation applied to both, with the method stated. Log and symmetric-log scales are not cosmetic switches. The chart should show whether a bound is physical, statistical or merely the display edge.

Compare groups without overclaiming

Overlap of two intervals is not a general significance test, and non-overlap is not the only way to establish a difference. If the decision concerns the difference between groups, estimate and plot that difference with its own interval. Signed differences put zero at the relevant comparison point. Check whether the same subjects appear in both groups; paired data require a paired calculation. For accessible reading, list each estimate and its endpoints in text, with units and the interval definition repeated where the chart may be shared alone.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def errorbar_distances(rows: list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]
                       ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]:
    names = [name for name, _, _, _ in rows]
    if len(names) != len(set(names)) or any(not name for name in names):
        raise ValueError("estimate labels must be unique and nonempty")
    output = []
    for name, estimate, lower, upper in rows:
        if not all(isfinite(value) for value in (estimate, lower, upper)):
            raise ValueError("estimate and bounds must be finite")
        if not lower <= estimate <= upper:
            raise ValueError("estimate must lie within its interval")
        output.append((name, estimate, estimate - lower, upper - estimate))
    return output

service_intervals = errorbar_distances([
    ("priority queue", 81, 59, 113),
    ("standard queue", 97, 83, 149),
])
assert service_intervals == [
    ("priority queue", 81, 22, 32),
    ("standard queue", 97, 14, 52),
]

Performance and operating cost

Preparing N intervals takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code validates geometry but cannot establish that endpoints were calculated with the right statistical method. Keep the original endpoints and method metadata even if the chart library wants only positive distances. Avoid computing an interval from a small sample with an unverified shortcut just because the renderer accepts two numbers.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling a range or standard deviation a confidence interval.
  • Forcing asymmetric endpoints into equal visual arms.
  • Clipping a bound at the axis edge without a marker or label.
  • Inferring a group-difference test only from overlap of separate intervals.

Validation drill

Show 59 response-time estimates with asymmetric intervals. Identify five bounds outside the current axis and revise the view without hiding those endpoints.

title: Proportional-symbol maps: size circles by area, not radius
summary: Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.
body:
Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.

A symbol has a location contract

A circle over a map may represent a precise facility, a regional centroid or an approximate address. Those are not equivalent. State what the coordinate means and how much location precision the data support. Choropleth maps color whole regions; proportional symbols encode a value at a point or chosen anchor. Do not place a regional total at a centroid without telling the reader that the circle summarizes an area. If location is sensitive, aggregate or coarsen before publication rather than relying on small marker size to conceal it.

Area should represent quantity

If a symbol encodes a nonnegative count, its visual area should be proportional to that count. Doubling the radius multiplies area by four, exaggerating the larger value. Compute radius from the square root of value relative to a declared maximum. Use a visible reference legend with at least two example magnitudes. A zero count should remain a recorded zero, even if its circle has no area; a tiny outline or table entry may be needed to keep the location discoverable. Scale integrity also means fixing the size domain across maps intended for comparison.

Overlapping circles need an explicit policy

Dense areas can hide smaller symbols under larger ones. Drawing order, opacity and zoom can all change what a reader sees. Try smaller maximum radius, outlines, clustering with disclosed counts, or an alternate ranked table. Do not let overlap remove records from the export. Hexbin density may be better when the question is where point events concentrate, while a proportional-symbol map is better when each point already has a meaningful aggregate. Test overlapping facilities at the closest supported zoom and on a narrow phone viewport.

Count and rate are different maps

A large population center may dominate a count map while having a modest per-person rate. A rate can be mapped with symbol size only if the legend names its denominator and the sampling uncertainty is not buried. Often a count-sized symbol plus a separately encoded rate is too much for one map; use paired maps or a table. The denominator contract must follow the geography and period. Export ID, coordinate meaning, count, denominator, computed rate, symbol radius and suppression state, so the map can be checked without its pixels.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def area_scaled_radii(values: dict[str, float],
                      maximum_radius: float) -> dict[str, float]:
    if not isfinite(maximum_radius) or maximum_radius <= 0:
        raise ValueError("maximum radius must be positive")
    if not values or any(not place for place in values):
        raise ValueError("locations must be named")
    if any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in values.values()):
        raise ValueError("mapped values must be finite and nonnegative")
    maximum_value = max(values.values())
    if maximum_value == 0:
        return {place: 0.0 for place in values}
    return {place: maximum_radius * sqrt(value / maximum_value)
            for place, value in values.items()}

service_calls = {"north depot": 47, "south depot": 188, "west depot": 0}
radii = area_scaled_radii(service_calls, 20)
assert radii["south depot"] == 20
assert radii["north depot"] == 10
assert radii["west depot"] == 0

Performance and operating cost

For N locations, finding the maximum and calculating radii takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code sizes nonnegative values by area and leaves geographic projection, collision handling and legend generation to the map renderer. A production map must keep one fixed reference maximum across views that readers are expected to compare; recalculating it after every filter changes apparent size.

Common Mistakes

  • Making radius proportional to count and thereby exaggerating area.
  • Treating a regional centroid as an exact event location.
  • Letting large symbols cover small ones without a table or overlap strategy.
  • Comparing maps whose size domains were auto-scaled independently.

Validation drill

Map 59 service depots with zero, small and large call counts. Use area-scaled circles, disclose the location meaning and produce a fixed-size legend for two reporting periods.

title: Choropleth maps: normalize counts and audit boundary coverage
summary: Join measures to the right polygons, use a stated denominator, and distinguish unmapped places from zero-valued regions.
body:
Join measures to the right polygons, use a stated denominator, and distinguish unmapped places from zero-valued regions.

Area color is not an event count

A choropleth fills geographic regions according to a measure. Large polygons occupy more pixels and can dominate attention even when they contain few people or events. Raw incident counts often track exposure, such as population or active deliveries, more than risk. For a comparable rate, carry numerator and denominator for each polygon and specify the period. Exposure-based rates explain why 8 incidents across 47,000 trips differ from 8 across 470 trips. A map can still show counts when workload is the question; label it as a count map.

Join by stable region identity

Names drift, abbreviations collide, and administrative boundaries change. Join facts to geometry with stable region IDs and a boundary version. Report unmatched fact IDs, polygons with no measure, duplicate assignments and overlapping boundaries before rendering. Spatial joins are a separate operation from coloring polygons; they can duplicate a record if geometries overlap. If one region splits midyear, a before-after map needs a common boundary basis or an explicit break. Do not let a chart library silently drop unmatched regions.

Projection and extent shape perception

A projection transforms coordinates into map space. It can distort area, shape or distance; no flat map preserves everything. For regional comparison, keep the same projection, extent and viewport across panels, and avoid interpreting the visible area of a polygon as its population. Insets for distant regions need clear labels and scale context. If exact comparison of rates matters more than location, provide a sorted bar chart alongside the map. Choose the visual that serves the question, not merely the available geometry.

Class breaks are an editorial decision

Equal-width bins, quantile bins and fixed policy thresholds answer different questions. A quantile palette can assign different colors to tiny numeric differences when many regions cluster tightly; fixed thresholds can leave some colors unused. Print numeric breakpoints and keep them stable when comparing dates. Use a separate treatment for missing data and low-exposure suppression. Color-domain rules carry over to map legends. Keep the original rate in the accessible table and tooltip; color bins are a summary, not the data.

Protect sensitive locations

Very small denominators can make rates unstable and expose information about a few people or facilities. Define a minimum publishable group size, aggregate or suppress as appropriate, and show a visible suppressed state. Do not infer that a blank region has zero risk. Location privacy and small-sample display belong to the same release review. Test a region with no geometry, a polygon with no observation, a zero numerator and a zero denominator separately.

Worked contract

def regional_rates(
    boundary_ids: set[str],
    incident_counts: dict[str, tuple[int, int]]
) -> dict[str, tuple[str, float | None]]:
    unknown = set(incident_counts) - boundary_ids
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"facts without geometry: {sorted(unknown)}")
    result = {}
    for region_id in boundary_ids:
        if region_id not in incident_counts:
            result[region_id] = ("missing", None)
            continue
        incidents, trips = incident_counts[region_id]
        if not 0 <= incidents <= trips:
            raise ValueError("invalid regional counts")
        result[region_id] = ("no-exposure", None) if trips == 0 else (
            "observed", incidents / trips)
    return result

rates = regional_rates({"zone-47", "zone-81", "zone-94"},
                       {"zone-47": (8, 470), "zone-81": (0, 81)})
assert rates["zone-47"][1] == 8 / 470
assert rates["zone-81"] == ("observed", 0.0)
assert rates["zone-94"] == ("missing", None)

Performance and operating cost

For B boundary IDs and M measured regions, this join-and-rate check takes O(B + M) expected time and O(B) output space using hash sets. Rendering cost depends on polygon vertex count, projection and viewport clipping, none of which this code performs. Simplify geometry only to a documented tolerance and keep an exact source for hit tests. A cached tile or geometry file must carry the same boundary version as the measures. The code distinguishes zero and missing; a real publication layer also enforces suppression and uncertainty policy.

Common Mistakes

  • Coloring raw counts as if the map showed per-person or per-trip risk.
  • Joining on human-readable region names without checking unmatched and duplicated keys.
  • Treating a missing polygon or missing measure as zero.
  • Changing map bounds or class breaks between comparison dates.

Validation drill

Map 23 service zones with one split boundary, one missing measure and one zone below the publishable exposure threshold. Reconcile region IDs and rates before drawing polygons; add a sorted rate table for exact comparison.

title: Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
summary: Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.
body:
Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.

A line implies continuity

A time-series chart maps measurements to ordered instants or calendar periods. Connecting two observed points across an unobserved day implies a path that was never measured. A recorded zero is different: it says the instrument or process observed the period and counted none. Store both the period key and an observation-status field before drawing the line. The observation calendar defines which periods were expected. Use a visible break, hollow mark, or separate missingness strip when a period has no measurement; do not silently replace it with zero.

Name the two clocks

Operational data often has an event timestamp and a processing timestamp. A refund received late may belong to Tuesday's customer cohort but be visible only on Thursday's dashboard. Choose the clock that answers the chart's question and label it in the axis or subtitle. When bucketing timestamps into local days, choose one time zone and convert before taking the date. Daylight-saving changes make a local day shorter or longer than 24 hours in some regions. An elapsed-duration chart should use instants; a calendar-day chart should use dates in the declared zone.

Mark provisional periods

A current day is incomplete even when its count is known so far. Drawing it with the same line and scale as closed days invites a false decline. Carry a finalized flag from the data source, and either exclude the open interval or render it with a different stroke and an explicit as-of time. Late corrections can reopen an earlier point, so the chart's data-version label matters. A reader must know whether yesterday is final, not only whether the plotting job ran.

Protect the comparison

Never join lines across a product outage, a changed population, or a denominator change without an annotation or split. Keep the y-axis unit and calculation stable across the displayed range. If one week contains 42, 47 and 51 eligible cases while the next has a different intake rule, raw counts compare different populations. The aggregation contract should produce both numerator and denominator where a rate is intended. A moving average may reduce noise, but its window, edge behavior and missing-day policy must be stated.

Check the drawn output

Test an interior missing day, an observed zero, an incomplete final day, a late revision, and a daylight-saving boundary for the region being displayed. Confirm that hover text, downloadable data and the axis all use the same period key. A chart-library setting that connects nulls can undo a carefully prepared missingness contract. Inspect the rendered image, not only the input array. The text alternative should report the gap and the as-of timestamp too.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(observed: dict[date, int],
                          start: date, end: date) -> list[tuple[date, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(count < 0 for count in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid date range or count")
    if any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("observation outside display range")
    return [(start + timedelta(days=offset),
             observed.get(start + timedelta(days=offset)))
            for offset in range((end - start).days + 1)]

points = complete_daily_series(
    {date(2026, 8, 11): 47, date(2026, 8, 13): 0},
    date(2026, 8, 11), date(2026, 8, 13))
assert [count for _, count in points] == [47, None, 0]

Performance and operating cost

For D expected periods and O observed keys, validation plus calendar completion takes O(D + O) time and O(D) output space. The code assumes an already chosen calendar zone and one authoritative count per day. Converting event timestamps and resolving duplicates belong upstream. For a long history, query only the visible interval, and keep finalization state beside each point; creating a million empty periods in a browser is a serving error, not a charting technique.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting an unobserved period into zero and drawing a continuous line.
  • Bucketing by server time zone while labeling the axis with the user's local dates.
  • Treating today's partial count as a completed daily value.
  • Using a rolling average without showing its window and missing-period rule.

Validation drill

Plot a 29-day refund series with one observed zero, two missing days and a provisional last day. Export the period keys and states, then verify that the line breaks only where observation is absent.

title: Chart annotations: align events to the right clock without claiming causality
summary: Treat deployment lines, policy changes and outages as versioned data with time windows and uncertainty.
body:
Treat deployment lines, policy changes and outages as versioned data with time windows and uncertainty.

An annotation is another dataset

A vertical line on a chart often marks a deployment, policy change or outage. That event has its own timestamp, time zone, scope, source and uncertainty. A release may roll through regions over several hours; drawing one instant across all regions invents precision. Model it as a window or per-region events, then map it to the same clock as the measured series. The time-series clock must be settled before annotations are placed.

Scope must match the measured population

If only one depot received a new workflow, an all-depot annotation can imply that every plotted change followed the intervention. Filter event records by affected site, product and population, and expose the scope in the label. Preserve events outside the visible interval in the export but do not draw them in the viewport. Distinguish a data outage from a true operational incident: both can create a cliff, but only one is a measured outcome. Population contracts determine whether a note belongs on a chart.

Timing does not prove effect

A change in the curve after a marked event may be coincidence, seasonality, a denominator shift or a delayed measurement. Write labels such as 'workflow enabled' rather than 'workflow improved response time' unless a separate analysis supports the latter. If an effect is being estimated, show the design, comparison group and uncertainty elsewhere. Effect-size analysis is distinct from descriptive annotation. Keep the event visible even when the post-event result disappoints expectations.

Avoid collision and preserve provenance

Several events on one day can produce overlapping labels. Group them in a visible list keyed to markers, prioritizing material scope and preserving access to every event. The annotation export should include event ID, earliest and latest time, scope, label and source version. A revised event time should update the chart and its manifest together. Reproducible exports need both series and annotation versions. Test daylight-saving boundaries and a deployment window that straddles the chart's range.

Worked contract

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def visible_events(
    events: list[tuple[str, datetime, datetime, set[str]]],
    view_start: datetime, view_end: datetime, depot_id: str
) -> list[str]:
    if view_start.tzinfo is None or view_end.tzinfo is None or view_start >= view_end:
        raise ValueError("invalid aware view interval")
    selected = []
    for event_id, began, ended, depots in events:
        if not event_id or began.tzinfo is None or ended.tzinfo is None or began >= ended:
            raise ValueError("invalid event interval")
        if depot_id in depots and began < view_end and ended > view_start:
            selected.append(event_id)
    return selected

utc = timezone.utc
window = [("release-47", datetime(2026, 8, 11, 9, tzinfo=utc),
           datetime(2026, 8, 11, 11, tzinfo=utc), {"north"})]
assert visible_events(window, datetime(2026, 8, 11, 10, tzinfo=utc),
                      datetime(2026, 8, 12, tzinfo=utc), "north") == ["release-47"]
assert visible_events(window, datetime(2026, 8, 11, 10, tzinfo=utc),
                      datetime(2026, 8, 12, tzinfo=utc), "south") == []

Performance and operating cost

Scanning E events is O(E) time and O(M) output space for M matching IDs. An indexed event store can narrow by time and scope for many dashboards. The example uses half-open display intervals and event windows, so a window ending exactly at the view start is excluded. It does not infer causality or validate whether a deployment reached every unit in its declared scope; those are separate evidence checks.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a gradual rollout as one global instant.
  • Annotating all depots with an event that affected only one.
  • Writing a causal outcome claim in an event label without a study.
  • Failing to version corrected event times alongside the plotted series.

Validation drill

Annotate a 29-day response-time chart with three region-specific rollouts, one data outage and one event that crosses the visible interval boundary. Verify the right events appear for each region and export their time windows.

title: Accessible charts: encode meaning without relying on color alone
summary: A chart needs legible labels, keyboard access where interactive, and a text route to the same substantive data.
body:
A chart needs legible labels, keyboard access where interactive, and a text route to the same substantive data.

Keep meaning redundant

A red and green pair is not enough to distinguish two completion series. Use direct labels, distinct line styles or marker shapes, and a legend that names the measured groups. Color can reinforce meaning but should not carry it alone. Axis labels must include units and remain legible at narrow widths.

Write a useful alternative

An image alternative should state the main comparison and notable exception, not simply “bar chart.” A companion table should expose exact values, periods and denominators for readers who cannot use the graphic. For an interactive chart, its filter controls need visible names, keyboard focus and a text update when the dataset changes.

Test the states

Check high zoom, narrow layout, monochrome output and keyboard-only interaction. A hover tooltip is not an adequate source of the only exact value. If a tooltip reports 74 percent but the accessible table says 73.6 percent, declare rounding once and use it consistently. Dashboard filters must update both representations together.

Budget complexity

A dense chart with 40 small labels may be technically accessible but still hard to scan. Reduce visible series, use a stable sort and provide a drill-down or table for detail. Retain disclosure of hidden groups and totals so simplification does not selectively remove an unfavorable channel.

Implementation

def chart_alt_text(period_label, channel_rates):
    measured = [(channel, rate) for channel, rate in channel_rates.items() if rate is not None]
    if not measured:
        return f"{period_label}: no channel has an eligible denominator."
    highest_channel, highest_rate = max(measured, key=lambda item: item[1])
    return (f"{period_label}: {len(measured)} channels measured; "
            f"{highest_channel} has the highest completion rate at {highest_rate:.1%}.")

Performance and operating cost

A short alternative over C channels costs O(C) time and O(C) temporary space in this implementation. For larger datasets, aggregate once and reuse the exact result for chart, table and alternative text to prevent divergence.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not rely on hue alone to identify a series.
  • Do not put the only exact value in a pointer-only tooltip.
  • Do not write alternative text from stale data after filters change.

title: Interactive dashboards: recompute cohorts after linked filters
summary: Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.
body:
Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.

A selection changes the population

Linked filtering lets a selection in one view constrain another. Clicking a depot, brushing a date range or choosing a channel changes the cohort behind every plotted metric. The interaction contract must specify whether filters combine with AND or OR, whether a second click toggles, and whether an empty selection means all or none. Show active filters in text and offer a clear reset. Dashboard provenance needs the same filter state that the user sees; otherwise a shared screenshot cannot be reproduced.

Recompute base counts

A precomputed overall completion percentage cannot simply be filtered and averaged. Reapply the filter to eligible records, then sum timely and eligible counts for the selected cohort. If a record appears in both a status log and an order table, deduplicate to the declared unit before counting. Grain and denominator rules are the invariant under interaction. A filtered group with zero eligible records should display an undefined rate and zero denominator, not a zero-percent success rate.

Synchronize every view

When a brush narrows a chart, its companion count, data table, map and export must use the same selected IDs or query predicate. Some dashboards filter the marks but leave the headline KPI unfiltered; users then compare incompatible populations. Carry one normalized state object and one data-version token into each query. If a backend response arrives after the user changes filters again, discard the stale response instead of replacing a newer view. A request ID or abort signal can enforce this. Large-series rendering may be approximate, but filter semantics must remain exact.

Make selection discoverable and reversible

Hover-only behavior hides controls from touch and keyboard users. Provide visible filter chips, keyboard-operable controls, focus cues and a readable selection summary. Color should not be the sole indication of selected marks. A reset should restore the documented default and preserve the date or snapshot policy, not silently switch to today's data. Accessible chart controls include data values outside the plotted canvas. Keep the browser back button or a shareable query state when deep analysis paths matter.

Test the state machine

Exercise no filters, one filter, two intersecting filters, mutually exclusive filters, a zero-eligible result, and rapid filter changes. Compare chart, KPI and export row counts for each state. For a selected region and channel, check that removing one chip broadens the cohort only along that dimension. Record the expected query predicate alongside a screenshot in a release test. If the chart is based on sampled or aggregated data, do not use a pixel brush to imply record-level exactness unless the backend can resolve it.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReviewRecord:
    receipt_id: str
    region: str
    channel: str
    eligible: bool
    timely: bool

def filtered_completion(records: list[ReviewRecord],
                        regions: set[str], channels: set[str]
                        ) -> tuple[int, int, float | None]:
    if len({record.receipt_id for record in records}) != len(records):
        raise ValueError("duplicate receipt identity")
    selected = [record for record in records
                if (not regions or record.region in regions)
                and (not channels or record.channel in channels)
                and record.eligible]
    if any(record.timely and not record.eligible for record in records):
        raise ValueError("timely receipt cannot be ineligible")
    timely = sum(record.timely for record in selected)
    eligible = len(selected)
    return timely, eligible, timely / eligible if eligible else None

receipts = [ReviewRecord("r-47", "north", "web", True, True),
            ReviewRecord("r-81", "north", "store", True, False),
            ReviewRecord("r-94", "south", "web", True, True)]
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"north"}, {"web"}) == (1, 1, 1.0)
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"south"}, {"store"}) == (0, 0, None)

Performance and operating cost

For N records, duplicate validation and filtering take O(N) expected time and O(N) temporary space in this direct version; the selected list can be avoided with streaming counters to use O(N) identity state and O(1) additional cohort state. For a remote dashboard, query cost and transfer volume usually dominate. Cache only by normalized filters, authorization context and data version. Never reuse a cached result across tenants or revisions merely because the visible filter chips match.

Common Mistakes

  • Filtering colored marks while leaving headline metrics on the full population.
  • Averaging cached percentages after a filter instead of summing base counts.
  • Treating an empty cohort as a measured zero-percent rate.
  • Letting an older network response overwrite the result of a newer selection.

Validation drill

Connect a weekly trend, region bar chart and completion KPI. Test six filter states and verify the same eligible count in the chart tooltip, KPI, table and CSV export for each state.
